extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, economists, and readers of political economy interested in trade and agricultural policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative criteria for judging trade restrictions, export/import regulations, monopolies, bounties, and the agricultural (land-focused) view of political economy as presented in a classical treatise. Useful for assessing whether a policy promotes consumers' welfare, creates perverse incentives, or properly attributes productive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and equality of treatment of different orders
rubrics_metrics.description: To hurt, in any degree, the interest of any one order of citizens, for no other purpose but to promote that of some other, is evidently contrary to that justice and equality of treatment which the sovereign owes to all the different orders of his subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should not intentionally disadvantage one social/economic class solely to benefit another; sovereign/government ought to treat different orders (producers, manufacturers, proprietors, cultivators) equitably. Example: prohibition of wool export hurts growers to promote manufacturers and is therefore unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer taxation to absolute prohibition on exportation
rubrics_metrics.description: These considerations...will not justify the absolute prohibition of the exportation of wool; but they will fully justify the imposition of a considerable tax upon that exportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming to protect domestic industry, impose a tax on exports instead of an outright ban: a tax raises sovereign revenue, hurts producers less than a prohibition, still gives domestic manufacturers relative advantage (lower cost than foreign competitors), and reduces illegal smuggling incentives compared with total prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid policies that create strong incentives to smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition, notwithstanding all the penalties which guard it, does not prevent the exportation of wool... The great difference between the price in the home and that in the foreign market, presents such a temptation to smuggling, that all the rigour of the law cannot prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations that produce large home/foreign price spreads (through bans or heavy export duties) will encourage illicit export/import. Good policy minimizes arbitrage opportunities or provides legal, taxed channels to limit contraband and ensure public revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption (consumer welfare) is the ultimate end of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumption is the sole end and purpose of all production; and the interest of the producer ought to be attended to, only so far as it may be necessary for promoting that of the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate policies primarily by their effect on consumers (prices, quality, availability). Policies that advantage producers at the cost of consumers (higher prices, reduced choice) are misplaced. Examples: import restraints and bounties that raise domestic prices to favor producers are criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice home consumers for producer advantages (protectionism/bounties) without net benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mercantile system, the interest of the consumer is almost constantly sacrificed to that of the producer... It is altogether for the benefit of the producer, that bounties are granted upon the exportation of some of his productions. The home consumer is obliged to pay, first the tax... and, secondly, the still greater tax which necessarily arises from the enhancement of the price of the commodity in the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing bounties, subsidies, or protectionist import duties, account for their distributional costs on consumers (higher prices, taxes to fund bounties) and avoid interventions where producer gains are outweighed by consumer losses and fiscal burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware manufacturer-imposed monopolies on materials and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as anything remains to be done, in order to fit any commodity for immediate use and consumption, our manufacturers think that they themselves ought to have the doing of it... Watch-cases, clock-cases, and dial-plates for clocks and watches, have been prohibited to be exported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions on exporting semi-manufactured materials, instruments of trade, or manufacturing inputs are typically instituted by manufacturers seeking to monopolize downstream processes; such restraints reduce competition, limit market access for primary producers, and should be evaluated for their anti-competitive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not restrain movement of skilled workers or knowledge for short-term manufacture protection
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 5th Geo. I. chap. 27, the person who shall be convicted of enticing any artificer... to go into any foreign parts, in order to practise or teach his trade, is liable... (heavy fines and imprisonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws that criminalize or penalize artisans from working abroad to prevent skill transfer hinder liberty and industrial improvement. Evaluate such policies for their injustice and inefficiency in preserving localized monopolies of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider full incidence of price changes on related market segments (quantity vs quality effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: This reduction of price... It may perhaps be thought, by discouraging the growing of wool, must have reduced very much the annual produce of that commodity... The growing of wool is not the chief purpose for which the sheep farmer employs his industry and stock. He expects his profit, not so much from the price of the fleece, as from that of the carcase... The goodness of the fleece depends, in a great measure, upon the health, growth, and bulk of the animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a policy's effect on output, analyze both quantity and quality channels and cross-price/income effects (e.g., lower fleece prices may not greatly reduce wool output if farmers primarily profit from meat; however, incentives to invest in fleece quality may decline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design import/export duty regimes coherently to avoid perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Our dyers, it seems, while they thought it for their interest to encourage the importation of those drugs, by an exemption from all duties, thought it likewise for their own interest to throw some small discouragement upon their exportation... It necessarily taught the importers to be more careful... that their importation should not exceed what was necessary for the supply of the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymmetric treatment of imports and re-exports (e.g., import duty exemptions but high export duties, no drawback) instructs traders to under-import, leading to scanty domestic supply and higher prices. Evaluate duty/drawback regimes for unintended supply restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for full public cost of colonial/imperial monopoly policies
rubrics_metrics.description: A great empire has been established for the sole purpose of raising up a nation of customers... For the sake of that little enhancement of price which this monopoly might afford our producers, the home consumers have been burdened with the whole expense of maintaining and defending that empire... more than two hundred millions have been spent, and a new debt of more than a hundred and seventy millions has been contracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating trade privileges tied to colonial monopolies, include defense and fiscal costs of maintaining such empires; small producer gains from monopoly may be vastly exceeded by public expenditures and debt service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify contributions to annual produce by economic role (proprietors/cultivators/artificers)
rubrics_metrics.description: They divide... into three classes: proprietors of land; the cultivators or productive class; artificers, manufacturers, and merchants, whom they... call the barren or unproductive class. The proprietors contribute by ground expenses; the cultivators by original and annual expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For analytical clarity, attribute types of contributions to economic output: proprietors' 'ground expenses' (improvements), cultivators' 'original' and 'annual' expenses (seed, instruments, maintenance). Use these categories to assess how policies affect each group's ability to contribute to annual produce.
